records.current_summary:
Goiás recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025 — a per-capita rate of about 0.69 per million per year against a population of ~7.2 million, roughly 1.8 times the national rate from that year's 80 national killings. For a trans visitor the operative risk factor is geographic: the national dossier finds most such killings occur in interior cities outside the capitals, where monitoring, reporting and access to public policy are weaker, and a visitor travelling beyond the capital shares that interior exposure.

No Goiás-specific ordinance, legal restriction or protection measure was identified in the audited sources; the risk profile therefore rests on the above-national per-capita killing count and the interior-concentration pattern rather than on any local legal hostility.

prison_adds.title: LGBT rights in Brazil (Wikipedia) - LGBTQ people in Brazilian prisons
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia's 'LGBT rights in Brazil' (fetched and read in full, 4 Oct 2026) states, in its Politics section, that LGBTQ people have a special place in Brazilian prisons, separate from other prisoners; that transsexuals have the right to be called by their social name and not their birth name and to be forwarded to women's prisons; and that LGBTQ people in prisons may choose male or female clothing. The sentence is footnoted to G1's 17 Apr 2014 report ('Governo publica portaria com direitos para presos gays e travestis', archived 12 Jul 2018) - i.e., the cited legal grounding is a 2014 federal portaria granting rights to gay and travesti prisoners. Placement axis: on paper, placement follows gender identity (trans prisoners forwarded to women's prisons), with separate custody for LGBTQ prisoners, social-name use and clothing choice; the underlying citation is dated (2014) and its current status was not independently re-verified.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ people in prison (Wikipedia) - Brazil section
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia overview article (fetched and read in full, 4 Oct 2026). Its Transgender issues > Brazil section contains no trans-prisoner placement rule - only discussion of social vulnerability, stigma and fragmented identity of travestis and transgender people during rehabilitation; international sections show placement norms elsewhere (e.g., Canada placing by gender identity, Italy's admission discretion). Negative evidence: this general overview documents no Brazil-specific trans-prisoner housing policy, special unit or segregation-for-placement practice.

records.current_summary:
Maranhão recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the same count the association dossier logged for it in 2024, so its position in the ranking's middle-upper band is persistent rather than a one-year spike. For a trans visitor the documented risk is structural exposure: two consecutive years of above-median lethal counts, a national victim profile concentrated in public places at night, and no local legal change either way.

No Maranhão-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement policy affecting trans people is documented in the audited sources; the national law applies uniformly, leaving no local legal hostility to weigh and no local protection beyond the national framework.

records.current_summary:
KwaZulu-Natal is where documented street violence against queer people meets the country's most powerful traditional authority. A 2024 criminology study from a university in the province documents queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minorities in KwaMashu, a township north of Durban — daily life in which the constitutional guarantee of equality does not reach. In January 2012 the Zulu King's anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival made the collision explicit: the royal house insisted the reported 'rotten' wording was a mistranslation; the South African Human Rights Commission said it would investigate; the provincial premier backed the royal family; and the Congress of Traditional Leaders of South Africa (CONTRALESA) responded that the Pietermaritzburg gay and lesbian network demanding an apology had shown the king 'disrespect' and was 'only seeking fame'.

For a discovered visitor, the province's pattern is that local moral authority — monarchy, chiefly councils, and the provincial government siding with them — has publicly ranged against queer claims, while academic documentation shows queerphobic violence persisting in its townships.

prison_adds.title: Transgender prisoners challenge prison authorities (GroundUp)
prison_adds.summary: GroundUp news feature (6 Aug 2025, Elna Schutz) documenting where transgender prisoners are held in South Africa: Jade September, a transgender woman, was imprisoned in the male section of Pollsmoor and won her 2019 Equality Court case against the Minister of Correctional Services, which ruled that not allowing her to express her gender identity was unfair discrimination. Reports that the resulting Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedure (SOP) for LGBT+ prisoners requires a safety-risk assessment within the first six hours of admission and stipulates that transgender men and transgender women are to be detained or transported only with other transgender men or transgender women respectively, alongside respectful-search and communication rules. Also notes Lawyers for Human Rights representation of 'NM', a transgender woman serving a long-term sentence at Johannesburg Correctional Centre, in litigation against DCS over gender-affirming healthcare, and rights organisations' concern about implementation of the SOP.

prison_adds.title: Nthabiseng Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre - Lawyers for Human Rights
prison_adds.summary: Lawyers for Human Rights case page (14 Nov 2025): the South African High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, ruled in favour of transgender inmate Nthabiseng Mokoena against the Department of Correctional Services (DCS), finding unfair discrimination and harassment because DCS refused to allow her to express her gender identity (feminizing attire, she/her pronouns) and failed to provide appropriate accommodation. The court held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at State expense, rejected DCS's contrary argument, and ordered DCS to immediately implement accommodations, enforce its own SOPs relating to transgender inmates, and provide the prescribed medical care. Subject-verified: documents that trans inmates are accommodated inside the standard national corrections system (here Johannesburg Correctional Centre) and that placement/accommodation obligations rest on DCS SOPs enforced through litigation.

prison_adds.title: Media Statement: National Preventive Mechanism welcomes the High Court ruling affirming the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities (SAHRC)
prison_adds.summary: South African Human Rights Commission, acting as the National Preventive Mechanism under OPCAT (designated 4 Dec 2024), media statement (14 Nov 2025) welcoming the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, judgment (delivered 10 Nov 2025) in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075). Describes Mokoena, assigned male at birth and identifying as female from early childhood, being restricted from wearing feminine clothing and makeup and misgendered while in a correctional facility. Subject-verified: an official state human-rights body confirming that transgender persons are held in the ordinary correctional system and that the 2025 ruling affirms their rights in correctional facilities, including accommodation.

records.current_summary:
Three LGBTIQ+ killings were recorded in this province in 2024, two of them suspected hate-crime murders of transgender people: on 14 May 2024 in Upington a 27-year-old transgender woman was stabbed multiple times and her body set on fire in her own room, discovered by a family member who noticed the house burning; on 1 June 2024 an 18-year-old transgender high-school student was stabbed more than 20 times in Kimberley after a man she had been drinking with allegedly turned on her on realising she was transgender. A third LGBTIQ+ person - a gay man - was killed in September 2024.

For a traveller, the exposure is severity-weighted: the methods are extreme and the province-level community shock is real, but the incidents are not clearly patterned or state-implicated, and no provincial legislative or enforcement finding against trans visitors is documented. Police opened murder cases in the first two killings - no arrests were reported at the first entry, and a suspect was reportedly arrested in the second (a claim the reporting could not verify with authorities). The register records that police 'identified' the first decedent by a deadname, an institutional practice a visibly trans traveller should anticipate. No visitor documents or border-screening practice is recorded in the dossier.

records.current_summary:
For a trans traveler Katsina is primarily a statutory-exposure record: it runs a religious criminal code, in operation since 20 June 2001, and the June 2025 government note confirms the code remains in force; it is one of only two states/provinces whose law carries death as the maximum penalty for same-sex acts between women as well as men.

Practical safety: no court-case study samples this state/province and no religious-police operation is documented for it, so enforcement here is the bloc-wide pattern rather than a locally documented record; no trans-specific incident is on record.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Nigeria (Wikipedia) - criminalisation layer incl. Katsina
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ rights in Nigeria' (fetched in full via MediaWiki API, cached research/fetched/815928c9a45eeba4.txt) documents the penalty structure relevant to any trans prisoner in Katsina: in the Shari'a-governed northern states punishments range from lashing/caning to capital punishment, and lesbianism (carnal acts or stimulation between women) is punishable by imprisonment or caning in most states with death penalties applied in Kano and Katsina. It also records the cross-dressing layer: men who dress or behave as women face prison or a fine, citing a 20 Jun 2025 Kano court sentence of a TikToker to one year in prison over a cross-dressing video. Placement axis: the article contains no statement on where trans prisoners are housed - no placement rule, no segregation or women's-wing policy, no Katsina prison-administration measure; it is a criminalisation/penalty record, not a housing record.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ people in prison (Wikipedia) - no Nigeria section
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia overview article (fetched in full via MediaWiki API, cached research/fetched/58ce7836f80217d1.txt). Full-text scan for 'Nigeria'/'Nigerian' returns zero mentions: the article's jurisdiction coverage (e.g., placement-by-gender-identity norms elsewhere) has no Nigeria entry. Negative evidence: the global overview documents no Nigeria- or Katsina-specific trans-prisoner housing policy, special unit or segregation-for-placement practice.
